sentences.text: Torosaurus was a massive ceratopsid that measured between 7.5 and 9 meters in length and weighed approximately 8 metric tons.
Other estimates suggest these individuals could have reached lengths of 9 meters and weights up to 11 metric tons.
The animal possessed an especially long skull due to its elongated frill.
This creature possessed one of the largest skulls found in any terrestrial animal.
The skull with the frill of Torosaurus measured approximately 2.8 meters in length.
Torosaurus was distinguished by an elongated frill with large fenestrae, long squamosal bones with a dorsal channel, and five or more pairs of epiparietal horns.
John Bell Hatcher estimated the skull of the type species holotype to be 2.2 meters long and the larger specimen to be 2.35 meters long.
The primary difference between Torosaurus and Triceratops was the shape of their frills.
Despite common belief, the name Torosaurus does not mean 'bull lizard' but rather 'perforated lizard', derived from the ancient Greek word for perforated.
A large specimen is considered a subadult because its unfused sutures and smooth bone texture indicate it was not fully grown despite its impressive size.
The genus Torosaurus was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1891.
In 1891, John Bell Hatcher discovered a pair of ceratopsian skulls with elongated, perforated frills in Niobrara County, southeastern Wyoming.
In 1891, two ceratopsian skulls with long frills perforated by large holes were found in southeastern Wyoming by John Bell Hatcher.
The paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh named the genus Torosaurus for these skulls.
In 1896, Marsh explained that the open perforations in the parietal bones suggested the name Torosaurus and separated it from other known ceratopsids.
The type species of the genus Torosaurus is Torosaurus latus.
The type species T. latus is based on holotype YPM 1830, which is a partial skull.
The holotype for the species T. gladius was specimen YPM 1831, which is an even larger skull than the type species.
Torosaurus has traditionally been classified in the subfamily Chasmosaurinae due to its long frill.
Cladistic analysis in the 1990s showed that both Torosaurus and Triceratops belong to the subfamily Chasmosaurinae.
Torosaurus belongs to the parent group Triceratopsini.
Torosaurus lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 72 to 66 million years ago.
Torosaurus lived during the Late Maastrichtian stage of the Cretaceous period.
Torosaurus lived during the Maastrichtian age in the Laramidia region.
Fossils of Torosaurus have been found across the Western Interior of North America, ranging from Saskatchewan to Texas.
Both fossils were found in the Lance Formation, which dates to the Maastrichtian stage.
In 2010, a study suggested that Torosaurus might represent the mature growth stage of Triceratops, characterized by an elongated frill and holes appearing during maturation.
In 2009, John Scannella proposed that Torosaurus and Triceratops were growth stages of the same genus based on his study of fossils in the Hell Creek Formation.
It is currently debated whether T. utahensis should be considered a distinct genus or the mature growth stage of a Triceratops species, similar to the hypothesis for T. latus.
Researchers consider the idea that Torosaurus frill holes formed after the bone was rejuvenated and granulated again to be an unlikely sequence.
In 1998, Thomas Lehman claimed that a Pentaceratops specimen had a skull that would have been 2.9 meters long in life.
